title: Making Inference Repeatable - Onepager
content:
Objective:
Provide a compact, product-centric positioning brief that reframes Redwood as the predictable, auditable, and cost-aware inference layer engineering teams adopt when model outputs must be repeatable and exceptions must be traced. This note is intended for PMM, sales enablement, and solutions engineering to use in decks and battlecards.

One-line positioning:
Redwood makes LLM behavior predictable at scale—so engineering teams can ship features with measurable economics, clear guardrails, and reproducible quality without operating the inference stack themselves.

Problem snapshot (2–3 bullets):
- LLM projects fail to scale because models are nondeterministic across environments, costs spike unpredictably, and debugging requires stitching traces from infra, prompts, and model versions.
- Platform teams lack primitives to reason about inference as a product-quality layer: they need repeatable correctness checks, cost-attribution per unit of behavior, and predictable degradation paths.
- Existing solutions focus on model access or raw throughput; customers want predictable decisioning (SLOs), audit trails for outputs, and operational levers to balance cost vs. quality.

Customer story (hypothetical):
- Payments product team at a fintech: uses Redwood to pin a reranker model version, enable prefix caching for frequent customer queries, enforce a fallback policy to cheaper quantized variants on high load, and retain token-level traces for compliance audits. Result: 40% reduction in variable inference spend on peak days and a reproducible incident postmortem for an anomalous prompt class.

Core thesis (why this matters now):
- As open models proliferate, owning the model is less durable than owning predictable serving. The real product risk is not accuracy per se, but inconsistent runtime behavior and opaque economics. Teams adopt Redwood when they need deterministic operational outcomes (latency, cost, traceability) in production.

Product pillars (short descriptions to reuse in messaging):
1) Predictable behavior: pin model versions, stable KV/prefix caching, deterministic routing rules, and replayable traces to reproduce any output.
2) Economics that map to outcomes: per-route cost views, batching/caching recommendations tied to latency SLOs, and fallback policies that trade cost for quality gracefully.
3) Observable correctness: token-level traces, prompt-set evals, regression alerts, and quality dashboards aligned to customer acceptance tests.
4) Portable control plane: same API and rollout semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private so customers can move without re-architecting controls.
5) Operational primitives for engineering teams: canary rollouts, automatic fallbacks, routing policies by cost/latency/region, and on-demand replay for debugging.

Differentiators — succinct phrases for GTM use:
- "Repeatability not just speed" — not only low latency but reproducible outputs and replayability.
- "Economics you can act on" — recommendations and controls that translate to predictable $/feature.
- "Auditable inference" — token-level traces and retention for compliance and SRE workflows.
- "Portable runtime controls" — identical developer surface across hosted/dedicated/private.

Proof points / supporting evidence to cite in collateral:
- Benchmarks: consistent p50/p95 latency across regional deployments in our internal suite (link to perf report).
- Cost impact: internal pilot with three customers showed median 28–45% unit-cost reduction using caching + dynamic batching.
- Reliability: fallbacks engaged in simulated outage drills preserved 93% of request success while shifting to cost-optimized variants.

Competitive implications (how to use in battlecards):
- Against cloud endpoints: emphasize operational primitives (traceability, predictable fallbacks) and lower variance in unit economics.
- Against self-hosted runtimes: emphasize the integrated control plane and SLAs for dedicated capacity; customers avoid building rollout/traceability tooling.
- Against model-access APIs: emphasize observability and the ability to pin/route between model variants without changing application code.

Key objections and rebuttals (sales-ready):
- "We can build this ourselves": Rebuttal — building kernel-optimized serving is one thing; building the guardrails (traceability, cost-controls, rollout semantics) that integrate with product SLOs is an order of magnitude of effort and maintenance.
- "We want custom stacks": Rebuttal — Redwood Private provides a portable control plane and can run in VPC/on-prem with KMS and audit logs; same developer surface, no lock-in at the app layer.

Quick assets to produce next (launch checklist):
- 1-page battlecard focused on "predictable outcomes" vs "model speed" with 3 short customer narratives.
- One-slide diagram showing control plane + runtime + observability and how rollback/fallback flows work.
- Short demo script for SEs: show pin + canary + replay to reproduce a failure.

Tone & audience guidance:
- Voice: pragmatic, engineering-first, outcome-driven. Avoid hype about model magic; focus on measurable production outcomes and operational controls.
- Primary audiences: product engineering leads, platform teams, SREs, and solution architects evaluating inference platforms.

Open questions / follow-ups for internal sync:
- Collect up-to-date anonymized metrics from three pilots to populate the "cost impact" proof point. (Owner: Solutions Eng)
- Finalize the single benchmark report link to include in collateral. (Owner: Performance team)
- Decide whether to surface fallbacks as a distinct product toggle or as part of rollout policies in the Console. (Owner: Product)

Usage notes:
- This brief is intentionally prescriptive: reuse short phrases under "Differentiators" verbatim in slides and one-pagers. Keep the customer story as a template for verticalized examples (fintech, commerce, support).

End of onepager.
